title: The Upside and Downside of Getting Pumped Up During Competition
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines "competitive arousal" — the psyched-up state performers display before and during high-stakes competition — and argues that, despite its popular image, it more often hurts performance than helps it. It walks through the cognitive costs: impaired rational decision-making, narrowed attention, increased risk-taking, and intensified bias, illustrated with examples from negotiation and gambling behavior. The piece does acknowledge a short-lived upside, the adrenaline-driven surge in energy and motivation, but frames it as fleeting and ultimately costly to execution and judgment. It closes by recommending performers pursue a steadier "controlled enthusiasm" instead of visible hype.
points: Competitive arousal has more downside than upside despite its dramatic, camera-friendly appearance in athletics.
Arousal impairs rational decision-making, narrows attention, increases risk-taking, and intensifies existing biases — with negotiators and gamblers a clear example.
The adrenaline/dopamine surge that makes performers feel 'superhuman' is real but brief, and its aftermath clouds judgment going forward.
The best performers favor a steady, 'controlled enthusiasm' over visible psych-up behavior.
quotes: Although common wisdom suggests getting pumped up during competition can, at certain moments, positively affect performance, research confirms that competitive arousal has more downside than upside.
Getting psyched up impairs rational and objective decision-making, narrows attention, increases risk-taking, and promotes aggressive behavior.
Once aroused, performers are more likely to fixate on winning at any cost, favoring immediate rewards over long-term benefits.
The flood of adrenaline and dopamine that performers experience during arousal makes them feel superhuman, if even for a moment.
That’s why the best performers manage their competitive arousal, preferring to stay focused and in control of their emotions in a more “controlled enthusiasm” while they perform.
